SEND
The school has a specialist Special Educational Needs Co-Ordinator (SENCo). This is Mrs Xaviera Bodkin. She works part time and is in school every Thursday. She can be contacted by phone via the school office, but because she works part time, it is advisable to do so via email. Her address is: xaviera.bodkin@stpetersaylesford.kent.sch.uk
Special Educational Needs and Disability
A child has SEND if they have a learning difficulty or disability which calls for special educational provision to be made for him or her. St Peter’s Church of England Primary School is committed to providing an inclusive education for all young people, regardless of ability, gender, language, ethnic or cultural origin. We work effectively with a wide variety of agencies and individuals to focus on improving outcomes for all children with Special Educational Needs. At St Peter’s Primary School we are committed to:
Please see our SEND Report giving details about what St Peter’s Primary School offers children with special educational needs.

Have you heard of the Local Offer? You can use this as a base to find information, support and services for children from 0-25 with special educational needs and disabilities and their families. pageCache.text:
Wrap Around Care
Wrap Around Care at St Peter’s is available for children attending the school. The facility is provided by St Peter’s School Wraparound Limited, which is a not for profit company (limited by guarantee) and is owned by the Governing Body of St Peter’s Church of England Primary School, and run by the Directors on their behalf. All of the staff employed in our wraparound provision are also employed in other roles within the school. The provision operates using school policies where needed. Hence, although this is a separate company, it is very much of the school. We run both a Breakfast and After School Club. These operate during term time only. There is no child care provision provided at St Peter’s during school holidays. Both the Breakfast and After School Clubs are based in the school hall. Breakfast Club runs from 7.30am and you can drop your child into the hall at any time from then onwards. We ask that you try to drop them before 8.15 if possible. It isn’t an enormous problem if you drop them after 8.15am, but it means that we have comparatively little time to settle the children and provide them with a breakfast before we have to pack away and get ready for the start of school at 8.30am. At 8.30am, the Breakfast Club staff will walk the children to their classrooms. Staff from the After School Club will collect our youngest children from their classes at the end of the day and take them to the hall. The older children make their own way to the hall. Once there, they will either enjoy a variety of activities in the hall if the weather is inclement, or if it is fine they will also have the option of going outside to play. At the Breakfast Club your child is provided with a variety of food and drink including cereals, toast and yoghurt. At the After School Club, you child receives a hot meal. All food and drink follow “Healthy Schools” guidelines. At the ASC we provide a wide range of activities for your child to take part in, including cookery, art and craft, board games, outdoor play and ICT. However, these are not “lessons” and children are free to choose a different activity to those on offer in consultation with the staff. The school site is secure and parents can only gain access onto the site by using the intercom system at the entrance gate on Mount Pleasant. To either drop your child at the Breakfast Club or to collect them from the ASC, operate the intercom and staff in the hall will release the gate lock to allow you to come in.
Session times
Sessions are run during Term Time. The precise dates of each term are issued annually. Please ask if you are unsure. Breakfast Club: 07:30 – Start of School After School Care: End of School – 18:00
Fees
We appreciate that some of you may not need to have your child stay after school and be fed by us. You may merely need time to get from your place of work, or from collecting older siblings, before you can get to our school. The extra 30-40 minutes you need doesn’t warrant paying for a full session at the ASC. Hence, we offer the one hour session for £5.50. Doing so, also assists those of you with 2 or more children, when one is staying for an extra-curricular club. If you wish, you’ll be able to have one child attend ASC for the hour that their sibling is in a club. The children who stay for just the hour won’t be fed. Bookings for Wraparound Care should be made online via the SchoolComms system. You must book a minimum of 7 days in advance. Only emergency sessions with less than 7 days’ notice will be booked by the office, if agreed by Wraparound Care staff. Short sessions can be booked right up to the day you need the provision (if there are spaces available), as we do not need to order food for the children attending these sessions. Breakfast and After School sessions need to be booked separately. Those who pay by bank transfer or cash will be asked for payment at the time of booking. We accept payment using Childcare vouchers. You will be able to book online and then send in your Childcare vouchers to the office. Fees are payable for all sessions booked, even if your child does not attend. Please note: late collections will be charged at the rate of £5 for every 10 minutes after 6:00 pm. Our staff work long days and have their own families to go home to, so please be on time to collect your child. We try to be as flexible as possible with regard to booking places at Wraparound. We appreciate that some working parents may receive quite short notice of their work patterns and hence their child care needs. Consequently we only ask for a minimum of one week’s notice when booking places at either the Breakfast Club or ASC. We need a week’s notice as we have to order the food we require for the number of children on each day. Of course, if you are certain of your child care needs, you can pre-book your sessions for a term or longer. However, conversely, if you have an emergency and need to use our Wraparound care at short notice, please call. We will always try to support you if we can. Neither the Breakfast Club nor ASC is at capacity so we do have spaces available if needed. Should the uptake rise considerably we will employ more staff to meet demand. If you have any questions or issues please call the school office who will be able to help.
The Wraparound Provision is inspected by Ofsted, just as the school is. Our last inspection was in 2021. The report can be viewed via the link below:
Wrap-Around-Care Ofsted Report 2021

House System
At St Peter’s we operate a very popular School House system. The children are divided into four House teams, Cossington (red group), Friars (green group), Medway (yellow group) and Kewlands (blue group). Siblings are always placed in the same house.
The children receive house points for good work and good behaviour. Each week, the house points are counted and the winner is announced in assembly. The cumulative points are kept and we have an overall winner each term.
Each house has its own captain and vice-captain, who are elected from Year 6 by their class mates. All of the staff are also members of the different houses. Only Mr Holditch is kept outside of this to ensure that he isn't tempted to announce the wrong winners at sports day. We have a sports day each summer and the winning house receives a trophy.
Each of the four houses is associated with one of the patron saints of the four countries making up the UK – Cossington has St George; Friars - St Patrick; Medway - St David, and Kewlands - St Andrew. On the patron saint’s feast day, the members of that particular house come to school out of uniform and wearing their house colour. They congregate at the flag pole at some stage during the day and raise their saint's flag.

Nurture UK Award
Nurture UK is a charity which has grown from the work in 1969 of a renowned educational psychologist, Marjorie Boxall. In a nutshell, her approach was to emphasise that schools needed to support the emotional needs of children and to address their general wellbeing, as a central part of their role. The value of this approach has long been recognised, and the DfE themselves focus on the need for schools to satisfy this role in the wider development of children.
St Peter’s has been recognised for the work we do in this regard. Nurture UK assess schools and just a very few receive accreditation as Nurturing Schools. Of the many thousands of schools in the South East of England, there were just 21 which have been awarded this accreditation. St Peter’s is now the 22nd.

Pupil Premium
Background to Pupil Premium Funding
In 2011-2012, the Government launched its Pupil Premium Funding. The Pupil Premium is allocated to both mainstream and non-mainstream schools for children who are of statutory school age and who satisfy at least one of certain criteria, namely: children who have been eligible for Free School Meals (FSM) at any point in the last 6 years; children who have been looked after continuously for more than six months; children adopted from care, and children whose parents are currently serving in the armed forces. The money is allocated to support initiatives aimed at ensuring that these pupils reach their full potential both academically and socially. However, we recognise that not all pupils who receive free school meals will be disadvantaged. We also recognise that not all pupils who are disadvantaged are registered or qualify for free school meals. Not all Pupil Premium children will be in receipt of interventions at any one time and some funding will be allocated to wider support mechanisms for the benefit of all. Schools are free to spend the Pupil Premium as they see fit. However, they will be held accountable for how they have used the additional funding to support Pupil Premium children.
Application of the Pupil Premium Funding
High quality teaching is fundamental to the outcomes for all of our pupils. Quality first teaching is the most important factor relating to pupil progression and closing the gap between the attainment levels of the disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils.
